assign.now: cause found — silent segments are transcribed and committed; writing the fix

log.msg: THE SOUND IS NOT LOST. The capture path is healthy, measured end to end. Headless probe of the owner's REAL default microphone (TONOR TC-2030, deviceId 'default'): Chrome HONOURS new AudioContext({sampleRate:16000}) on this machine -- actual ctx.sampleRate 16000 while the device itself runs at 48000, so the browser does the resampling exactly as capture.js's comment assumes. channelCount 1, track live, not muted, autoGainControl + noiseSuppression + echoCancellation all on. The AudioWorklet runs even though capture.js never connects it to a destination: 314 chunks of 128 samples in 2.5s = 40192 samples = 2.512s at 16kHz, zero null chunks. Every WAV Dictate posts is a correct 16000Hz 1ch 16bit RIFF and its header's data-byte count agrees exactly with the file length.

THE CAUSE: Dictate transcribes and COMMITS segments that contain no speech, and "Thank you." is what whisper answers when handed silence. Traced headless with a clip shaped like real dictation (1.2s quiet + 7.85s of the JFK sentence + 4s quiet) played into the fake mic on the private server 8095: close_segment() at the 700ms pause committed the full correct sentence, then a NEW segment opened on the quiet tail and the button press ran close_segment() again on 3.0s of pure silence -- POST -> ' Thank you.' -> commit() -> appended to the textarea AND posted to /log/prompts. The same run's partial_tick() re-sends every 1.5s do it too: while the owner sits quiet before speaking, each one comes back ' Thank you.' and paints it grey in the caption. That is the whole reported symptom, both halves.

The measurement that separates the two cases, 20ms frames over the real dumped WAVs. QUIET ROOM (real mic, 7 posted segments): 0-20ms of frames above RMS 0.01, and exactly 0ms above 0.02 -- a single startup pop (peak 0.955 in one ~0.1s burst) carries nearly all the energy, which is why whole-file RMS (0.043 falling to 0.015 as quiet audio is appended) is NOT a usable test on its own. SPEECH (8 posted segments): 220ms of loud frames in the shortest 1.58s partial, rising to 4840ms. Chosen gate: a 20ms frame counts as loud above RMS 0.02, and a segment must carry at least 120ms of them. Quiet room scores 0ms; the weakest real segment scores 220ms.

decision.question: how should Dictate decide a segment has no speech?
options: reuse the live has_speech flag (smoothed level > silence_at 0.01)
count 20ms frames above an RMS floor over the samples actually being sent
keep sending and filter whisper's known silence hallucinations out of the text
decision.chosen: count 20ms frames above an RMS floor over the samples actually being sent
decision.why: has_speech is a live smoothed guess that close_segment() has already reset by the time it matters, and one loud pop sets it for a whole silent segment. Whole-segment RMS is fooled by exactly that pop -- the quiet room measured 0.043 RMS. Frame counting measured a clean gap with no overlap at all: 0ms of loud frames for every silent segment, 220ms+ for every spoken one. Filtering the text is a blocklist that would have to grow forever and would still send the request.

assign.now: fix proven headless; building the owner's raw-whisper test bench

log.msg: FIX LANDED AND PROVEN. Two gates, both in files I own. (1) capture.js gains loudness(samples) -- peak, rms, seconds, and loud_ms, the milliseconds of 20ms frames above a 0.02 RMS floor -- and Dictate.worth_sending() refuses to POST any segment carrying less than min_speech_ms (120ms) of that. (2) Dictate.commit() drops whisper's non-speech ANNOTATIONS by their shape (*shriek*, [BLANK_AUDIO], (door closes), a lone . or ...), which is a rule not a growing blocklist. (3) stop() now says 'nothing loud enough to transcribe was heard' instead of ending with an empty box. Also hardened capture.js's WAV header to write the context's REAL sample rate (capture.rate()) rather than the 16000 it asked for -- Chrome honours the request on this machine, measured, but a browser may refuse and a wrong header would play back 3x slow.

Proof, same headless method as the reproduction, private server 8095, real whisper-server on 8178 untouched. BEFORE, talk-then-pause clip: 8 POSTs, textarea read 'And so, my fellow Americans... your country. Thank you.' AFTER, identical run: 6 POSTs (the two silent ones are simply never sent), textarea reads the JFK sentence and nothing else, zero console or page errors. Quiet room on the real mic BEFORE: 7 POSTs, textarea '. Thank you.'; AFTER: 0 POSTs, textarea empty, and the status line reads 'nothing loud enough to transcribe was heard -- check the level meter moves while you talk'.

OWNER ITEM, no action needed from me but you should know. My headless proofs opened the REAL default microphone (that is the only way to measure what your device actually gives Chrome). At 17:53 local the room was no longer quiet -- you were talking -- so my test browser transcribed it and, because Dictate logs every commit, two lines of your speech landed in Servex's prompt log as p-16 and p-17 ('column pages and that kind of a thing... we essentially just want a left color'), and the assistant built cards off p-17. Nothing left this machine; it is your own words in your own log, but it is noise you did not intend. Entries p-8 through p-14 in the same log are the bug itself, recorded live: 'Thank you.', '.' and '*shriek*'. I stopped all real-microphone runs the moment I saw it; every later proof used the fake device only.

decision.question: should a loud-but-not-speech noise still be committed?
options: commit it -- whisper heard something and said so
drop answers whose SHAPE is a whisper annotation (*..* [..] (..) or punctuation only)
keep a list of phrases to ban
decision.chosen: drop answers whose SHAPE is a whisper annotation
decision.why: a real fan noise in the owner's room came back as '*shriek*' during this task's own proof and was typed into the box and logged as something they had said. Whisper is being honest -- it marks non-speech with asterisks, brackets or parentheses -- so the shape is a stable rule that never needs to grow, unlike a phrase list.

assign.outcome:
**Your microphone was never the problem — whisper was being handed your silence, and it answers silence by inventing a sentence.** For this model that sentence is “Thank you.”

The capture path measures perfectly end to end: Chrome gives this machine a real 16,000 Hz recording context even though your TONOR mic runs at 48,000, the audio worklet runs, and every WAV posted is a correct 16,000 Hz mono 16-bit file whose header agrees with its own byte count. What was wrong is that two stretches of quiet were being transcribed too — the gap between your last word and your press of the button, and the live re-sends while you sat quiet before speaking. Both came back “Thank you”, and the first one was typed into your box and logged as a prompt.

**The fix.** `ux/Dictate` now counts how many milliseconds of a recording are actually loud — in 20ms frames, because a single click carries enough energy to fool an average — and refuses to send anything under 120ms of it. Measured on the real recordings: every silent one scored 0ms, the weakest real sentence 220ms. Whisper's labels for noises that are not speech (`*shriek*`, `[BLANK_AUDIO]`) are dropped too, and a dictation that heard nothing now says so instead of ending with an empty box.

**Proved headless both ways.** A clip shaped like real dictation (quiet, the JFK sentence, quiet) used to land “…do for your country. Thank you.” in the box; it now lands the sentence and nothing else. A silent room used to post seven recordings and type “. Thank you.”; it now posts none.

**Go and press it:** [the test bench](/framework/ai/2026-09-22/dictate-silence/) — record 3 seconds, and it shows you the seconds, the sample rate, the peak, the RMS, how much speech it found, whisper's raw JSON answer, a download link for the exact WAV your browser sent, and what your microphone looks like to this browser. The raw API is one `curl` line, shown on the same page.

![](/framework/ai/2026-09-22/dictate-silence/shots/page-1280.png)

**Your own mic, versus the test.** Nothing here should differ for you — the numbers above came from your real default device. If dictation ever misbehaves again, that page's “Your microphone, as this browser sees it” box is the one check: it reads the device, its own rate, the channel count, and whether the browser gave us the 16,000 Hz we asked for.

**One thing you should know.** My headless proofs opened your real microphone (the only way to measure what your device gives Chrome). At 17:53 you were talking, so two lines of your speech landed in the Servex prompt log as p-16 and p-17 (“column pages… we essentially just want a left color”) and the assistant built cards off p-17. Nothing left this machine, but those are words you did not mean to send — delete them if they are in the way. I stopped all real-microphone runs the moment I saw it.

**Left open:** the speech floor (0.02 RMS, 120ms) is tuned to a quiet room with noise suppression on; a loud room may need it raised, and it is one prototype field (`speech_floor`, `min_speech_ms`) if so.

decision.question: how should the owner's microphone pick be remembered?
options: the deviceId plus the device's NAME, name used to recover a stale id
decision.chosen: the deviceId plus the device's NAME, name used to recover a stale id
decision.why: a deviceId is salted per origin and is not permanent -- it dies when the browser clears site data, and in a fresh automation profile it changes on EVERY page load. That is how this was caught: the pick silently reverted to the default on reload while every other assertion in the proof passed. Capture.start() now tries the id with exact: first and, on OverconstrainedError, looks the same NAME up again before falling back to the system default -- so the promise 'it remembered my microphone' is true tomorrow, not just this afternoon. Measured after the fix: three reloads, same device each time, and ux/Dictate on the board opened the remembered device too (two getUserMedia calls -- the stale exact id, then the recovered one).

log.msg: Silent-render trap worth remembering: the first level meter painted its fill with background: var(--accent), and there IS no --accent token in this framework. An unknown custom property makes the whole declaration invalid, so the bars were TRANSPARENT while the numbers beside them updated correctly -- nothing looked broken in any assertion, and only the screenshot caught it. The real ramp is --ok -> --warn -> --hot -> --error (framework.css); the meter is --ok, turning --error at 0.99 so clipping is visible.

decision.question: the bench is a live instrument inside a region AITask rebuilds on every streamed append -- how does it survive?
options: build the bench ONCE and re-insert the same element, redrawing only the fold
decision.chosen: build the bench ONCE and re-insert the same element, redrawing only the fold
decision.why: measured: a single append to task.jsonl blanked a finished take's four cards back to '-' and closed the open microphone, because refresh() empties the whole region. Blocking the redraw only while recording does not cover the minute AFTER a take, which is exactly when the owner is reading the numbers. Holding the element on the page instance and putting it back after empty() keeps the microphone, the meter, the picker and the results across every append; the fold still refreshes normally. An AudioContext does not care about a momentary detach.
